claim: Dopamine and striatal dysfunctions play a key role in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease (PD) and Dystonia.
source: Dopamine and striatal dysfunctions play a key role in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease (PD) and Dystonia, but our understanding of the changes in the discharge rate and pattern of striatal projection neurons (SPNs) remains limited.
evidence: This is a statement about established understanding in the field, drawing from general scientific knowledge about these disorders.

claim: The understanding of changes in the discharge rate and pattern of striatal projection neurons (SPNs) in PD and Dystonia remains limited.
source: Dopamine and striatal dysfunctions play a key role in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease (PD) and Dystonia, but our understanding of the changes in the discharge rate and pattern of striatal projection neurons (SPNs) remains limited.
evidence: This statement acknowledges gaps in current scientific understanding.

claim: No drastic changes were found in the spontaneous discharge of well-isolated and stationary SPNs of PD patients compared to dystonic patients.
source: Contrary to earlier human findings, we found no drastic changes in the spontaneous discharge of the well-isolated and stationary SPNs of the PD patients compared to the dystonic patients or to the normal levels of striatal activity reported in healthy animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data from recordings in PD and dystonic patients.

claim: No drastic changes were found in the spontaneous discharge of well-isolated and stationary SPNs of PD patients compared to normal levels of striatal activity reported in healthy animals.
source: Contrary to earlier human findings, we found no drastic changes in the spontaneous discharge of the well-isolated and stationary SPNs of the PD patients compared to the dystonic patients or to the normal levels of striatal activity reported in healthy animals.
evidence: This finding is based on comparison of current data with previously published data from healthy animals.

claim: Cluster analysis using SPN discharge properties did not characterize two well-separated SPN subpopulations in PD or Dystonia.
source: Moreover, cluster analysis using SPN discharge properties did not characterize two well-separated SPN subpopulations, indicating no SPN subpopulation-specific (D1 or D2 SPNs) discharge alterations in the pathological state.
evidence: This is a finding from cluster analysis performed on the experimental data.

claim: There are no SPN subpopulation-specific (D1 or D2 SPNs) discharge alterations in the pathological state of PD and Dystonia.
source: Moreover, cluster analysis using SPN discharge properties did not characterize two well-separated SPN subpopulations, indicating no SPN subpopulation-specific (D1 or D2 SPNs) discharge alterations in the pathological state.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cluster analysis results.

claim: Small to moderate changes in spontaneous SPN discharge related to PD and Dystonia are likely amplified by basal ganglia downstream structures.
source: Our results imply that small to moderate changes in spontaneous SPN discharge related to PD and Dystonia are likely amplified by basal ganglia downstream structures.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results regarding how small changes might lead to clinical symptoms.

claim: PD is traditionally attributed to the degeneration of midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
source: Traditionally, PD is attributed to the degeneration of the midbrain dopaminergic neurons which also disrupts other neuromodulary systems, including the cholinergic, serotoninergic and histaminergic systems (Bolam and Ellender, 2016; Deffains and Bergman, 2015; Fox et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by citations.

claim: Degeneration of midbrain dopaminergic neurons in PD disrupts other neuromodulatory systems, including the cholinergic, serotoninergic and histaminergic systems.
source: Traditionally, PD is attributed to the degeneration of the midbrain dopaminergic neurons which also disrupts other neuromodulary systems, including the cholinergic, serotoninergic and histaminergic systems (Bolam and Ellender, 2016; Deffains and Bergman, 2015; Fox et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: There is no degeneration of midbrain dopaminergic neurons in Dystonia.
source: Although there is no degeneration of the midbrain dopaminergic neurons in Dystonia, an imbalance between the midbrain dopaminergic and striatal cholinergic systems (Aosaki et al., 2010; Benarroch, 2012; Bonsi et al., 2011; Pisani et al., 2007), as well as cerebellum dysfunction (Fremont et al., 2017; Helmich, 2018; Helmich et al., 2012; Tewari et al., 2017; Wu and Hallett, 2013) are present in both PD and Dystonia.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of Dystonia supported by the literature.

claim: An imbalance between the midbrain dopaminergic and striatal cholinergic systems is present in both PD and Dystonia.
source: Although there is no degeneration of the midbrain dopaminergic neurons in Dystonia, an imbalance between the midbrain dopaminergic and striatal cholinergic systems (Aosaki et al., 2010; Benarroch, 2012; Bonsi et al., 2011; Pisani et al., 2007), as well as cerebellum dysfunction (Fremont et al., 2017; Helmich, 2018; Helmich et al., 2012; Tewari et al., 2017; Wu and Hallett, 2013) are present in both PD and Dystonia.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cerebellum dysfunction is present in both PD and Dystonia.
source: Although there is no degeneration of the midbrain dopaminergic neurons in Dystonia, an imbalance between the midbrain dopaminergic and striatal cholinergic systems (Aosaki et al., 2010; Benarroch, 2012; Bonsi et al., 2011; Pisani et al., 2007), as well as cerebellum dysfunction (Fremont et al., 2017; Helmich, 2018; Helmich et al., 2012; Tewari et al., 2017; Wu and Hallett, 2013) are present in both PD and Dystonia.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Basal ganglia (BG) dysfunction is regarded as the source of the cardinal symptoms of both PD and Dystonia.
source: Nevertheless, basal ganglia (BG) dysfunction is still regarded as the source of the cardinal symptoms of both diseases (Mink, 1996; Wichmann, 2018) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) in the BG (subthalamic nucleus, STN and internal segment of the globus pallidus, GPi) is an effective invasive treatment for both diseases (Limousin et al., 1998; Moro et al., 2017; Odekerken et al., 2016; Ostrem et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a widely accepted view in the field supported by citations.

claim: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) in the BG (subthalamic nucleus, STN and internal segment of the globus pallidus, GPi) is an effective invasive treatment for both PD and Dystonia.
source: Nevertheless, basal ganglia (BG) dysfunction is still regarded as the source of the cardinal symptoms of both diseases (Mink, 1996; Wichmann, 2018) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) in the BG (subthalamic nucleus, STN and internal segment of the globus pallidus, GPi) is an effective invasive treatment for both diseases (Limousin et al., 1998; Moro et al., 2017; Odekerken et al., 2016; Ostrem et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by clinical evidence cited in the literature.

claim: The striatum is the main input structure of the BG network.
source: The striatum (i.e., the main input structure of the BG network) is the main recipient of midbrain dopaminergic neurons (Menegas et al., 2015) and also receives di-synaptic cerebellar projections (Bostan et al., 2013; Hoshi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact.

claim: The striatum is the main recipient of midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
source: The striatum (i.e., the main input structure of the BG network) is the main recipient of midbrain dopaminergic neurons (Menegas et al., 2015) and also receives di-synaptic cerebellar projections (Bostan et al., 2013; Hoshi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The striatum receives di-synaptic cerebellar projections.
source: The striatum (i.e., the main input structure of the BG network) is the main recipient of midbrain dopaminergic neurons (Menegas et al., 2015) and also receives di-synaptic cerebellar projections (Bostan et al., 2013; Hoshi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Most striatal neurons are medium spiny projection neurons (SPNs), comprising ~95% in rodents and ~70-80% in primates.
source: Most [~95% and~70–80% in rodents and primates, respectively (Graveland et al., 1985; Petryszyn et al., 2018; Petryszyn et al., 2014)] striatal neurons are medium spiny projection neurons (SPNs) that receive afferents from the cortex and the thalamus, and together with the STN neurons, innervate the central (i.e., external segment of the globus pallidus, GPe) and output (i.e., GPi and substantia nigra reticulata, SNr) BG structures (Albin et al., 1989; Gerfen et al., 1990).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact supported by citations.

claim: SPNs receive afferents from the cortex and the thalamus.
source: Most [~95% and~70–80% in rodents and primates, respectively (Graveland et al., 1985; Petryszyn et al., 2018; Petryszyn et al., 2014)] striatal neurons are medium spiny projection neurons (SPNs) that receive afferents from the cortex and the thalamus, and together with the STN neurons, innervate the central (i.e., external segment of the globus pallidus, GPe) and output (i.e., GPi and substantia nigra reticulata, SNr) BG structures (Albin et al., 1989; Gerfen et al., 1990).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact supported by citations.

claim: SPNs, together with STN neurons, innervate the central (GPe) and output (GPi and SNr) BG structures.
source: Most [~95% and~70–80% in rodents and primates, respectively (Graveland et al., 1985; Petryszyn et al., 2018; Petryszyn et al., 2014)] striatal neurons are medium spiny projection neurons (SPNs) that receive afferents from the cortex and the thalamus, and together with the STN neurons, innervate the central (i.e., external segment of the globus pallidus, GPe) and output (i.e., GPi and substantia nigra reticulata, SNr) BG structures (Albin et al., 1989; Gerfen et al., 1990).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact supported by citations.

claim: Alterations in striatal signaling disrupt normal BG activity and may lead to the manifestation of motor and non-motor symptoms of PD and Dystonia.
source: Therefore, alterations in striatal signaling disrupt normal BG activity and may lead to the manifestation of the motor and non-motor symptoms of PD and Dystonia (Albin et al., 1989; Bergman et al., 1990; Gerfen et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: Extracellular recordings of spiking activity in non-human primates (NHPs) reveal that SPNs have a very low discharge rate (~1–2 Hz at rest).
source: Unlike in all other BG structures, extracellular recordings of spiking activity in non-human primates (NHPs) reveal that SPNs have a very low discharge rate (~1–2 Hz at rest) and are phasically active (i.e. emit short bursts) around relevant behavioral events (Crutcher and DeLong, 1984; Deffains et al., 2010; Kimura et al., 1990).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental data from NHP studies.

claim: SPNs are phasically active (emit short bursts) around relevant behavioral events.
source: Unlike in all other BG structures, extracellular recordings of spiking activity in non-human primates (NHPs) reveal that SPNs have a very low discharge rate (~1–2 Hz at rest) and are phasically active (i.e. emit short bursts) around relevant behavioral events (Crutcher and DeLong, 1984; Deffains et al., 2010; Kimura et al., 1990).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental data from NHP studies.

claim: Previous studies of the BG in the NHP model of PD have mainly focused on the STN, GPe and GPi which have a high frequency tonic discharge (25–70 Hz at rest).
source: However, previous studies of the BG in the NHP model of PD have mainly focused on the STN, GPe and GPi which are structures with a high frequency tonic discharge (i.e. 25–70 Hz at rest) (Deffains et al., 2016; Filion and Tremblay, 1991; Wichmann and DeLong, 2003).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: Studies have reported excessive GPi/SNr discharge rates in PD that lead to an increase in BG inhibitory outputs to the thalamus and the frontal cortex motor areas.
source: These studies have reported excessive GPi/SNr discharge rates in PD that lead to an increase in BG inhibitory outputs to the thalamus and the frontal cortex motor areas (Wichmann and DeLong, 2003).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: It is assumed that Dystonia (and other hyper-kinetic states) are characterized by reduced GPi/SNr activity.
source: Conversely, it is assumed that Dystonia (and other hyper-kinetic states) are characterized by reduced GPi/SNr activity (Guehl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption supported by citation.

claim: Parkinsonism-related β oscillations have been observed in local field potentials (LFPs) recorded in all BG structures, including the striatum.
source: Parkinsonism-related β oscillations have been observed in local field potentials (LFPs) recorded in all BG structures, including the striatum (Deffains et al., 2016; Kondabolu et al., 2016; Lemaire et al., 2012; Singh and Papa, 2019).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claim: Low frequency (4–12 Hz) LFP oscillations have been recorded in the BG network of dystonic patients.
source: Similarly, low frequency (4–12 Hz) LFP oscillations have been recorded in the BG network of dystonic patients (Piña-Fuentes et al., 2018; Silberstein et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claim: Synchronous β oscillations are commonly observed in the spiking activity of the STN, GPe and GPi of MPTP-treated monkeys.
source: Finally, synchronous β oscillations are commonly observed in the spiking activity of the STN, GPe and GPi of MPTP-treated monkeys (Deffains et al., 2018; Deffains et al., 2016; Soares et al., 2004) and PD patients (Brown, 2003; Kuhn et al., 2005; Moshel et al., 2013; Zaidel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claim: Synchronous β oscillations are commonly observed in the spiking activity of the STN, GPe and GPi of PD patients.
source: Finally, synchronous β oscillations are commonly observed in the spiking activity of the STN, GPe and GPi of MPTP-treated monkeys (Deffains et al., 2018; Deffains et al., 2016; Soares et al., 2004) and PD patients (Brown, 2003; Kuhn et al., 2005; Moshel et al., 2013; Zaidel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claim: Previous studies utilizing the NHP model of PD reported striking increases (~15 fold increase from the normal discharge rate of ~1–2 Hz) in the firing rate of the SPNs subsequent to striatal dopamine depletion and the induction of parkinsonism.
source: Previous studies utilizing the NHP model of PD reported striking increases (~15 fold increase from the normal discharge rate of ~1–2 Hz) in the firing rate of the SPNs subsequent to striatal dopamine depletion and the induction of parkinsonism (Liang et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on cited previous research.

claim: A research group reported a high discharge rate of SPNs recorded in PD and dystonic patients (~30 Hz and 9 Hz, respectively).
source: The same research group also reported a high discharge rate of SPNs recorded in PD and dystonic patients (~30 Hz and 9 Hz, respectively) (Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on cited previous research.

claim: A significant change in the firing pattern of striatal neurons was found, with many SPNs exhibiting bursting activity in PD patients and MPTP monkeys as compared to a smaller fraction in patients with Dystonia.
source: They also found a significant change in the firing pattern of striatal neurons, with many SPNs exhibiting bursting activity in PD patients and MPTP monkeys as compared to a smaller fraction in patients with Dystonia (Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on cited previous research.

claim: The SPNs of patients with essential tremor (ET) have a very low discharge rate (~2 Hz) and no tendency to burst, as reported in normal NHPs.
source: Finally, the SPNs of patients with an essential tremor (ET, regarded as a non-BG disorder) have a very low discharge rate (~2 Hz) and no tendency to burst, as reported in normal NHPs (Liang et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on cited previous research.

claim: The authors' research group recorded the activity of SPNs and other BG neurons in Vervet monkeys before and after systemic MPTP treatment and the induction of severe parkinsonian symptoms.
source: We recorded the activity of SPNs and other BG neurons in Vervet monkeys before and after systemic 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) treatment and the induction of severe parkinsonian symptoms.
evidence: This describes the authors' own experimental work.

claim: The authors found robust changes in the discharge properties (rate, pattern and synchronization) of the STN, GPe and BG output structures in MPTP-treated monkeys.
source: Although we found robust changes in the discharge properties (rate, pattern and synchronization) of the STN, GPe and BG output structures, we did not observe any difference in the discharge rate (~2–3 Hz) or pattern of SPNs in the MPTP-treated monkeys in comparison to the recordings in the same monkeys before MPTP treatment (Deffains et al., 2018; Deffains et al., 2016; Deffains and Bergman, 2019).
evidence: This is based on the authors' own experimental data.

claim: The authors did not observe any difference in the discharge rate (~2–3 Hz) or pattern of SPNs in MPTP-treated monkeys in comparison to the recordings in the same monkeys before MPTP treatment.
source: Although we found robust changes in the discharge properties (rate, pattern and synchronization) of the STN, GPe and BG output structures, we did not observe any difference in the discharge rate (~2–3 Hz) or pattern of SPNs in the MPTP-treated monkeys in comparison to the recordings in the same monkeys before MPTP treatment (Deffains et al., 2018; Deffains et al., 2016; Deffains and Bergman, 2019).
evidence: This is based on the authors' own experimental data.

claim: Extracellular recordings of SPN spiking activity of anesthetized and awake rats before and after striatal dopamine depletion by 6-OHDA treatment have revealed a significant, but very slight increase in the SPN discharge rate.
source: Extracellular recordings of SPN spiking activity of anesthetized (Chen et al., 2006; Mallet et al., 2006; Sharott et al., 2017) and awake (Chen et al., 2006; Kish et al., 1999) rats before and after striatal dopamine depletion by 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) treatment have revealed a significant, but very slight increase in the SPN discharge rate.
evidence: This is based on cited rodent studies.

claim: A significant imbalance in the discharge rate and calcium dynamics of D1 and D2 SPNs was observed in the dopamine-depleted striatum.
source: A significant imbalance (but see Ketzef et al., 2017) in the discharge rate and calcium dynamics of D1 and D2 SPNs was observed in the dopamine-depleted striatum (Mallet et al., 2006; Parker et al., 2018; Sharott et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on cited rodent studies, with a caveat noted.

claim: D2 SPNs increased their discharge in the dopamine-depleted striatum.
source: In particular, D2 SPNs increased their discharge (Mallet et al., 2006; Sharott et al., 2017) and were also prone to being entrained to parkinsonian β oscillations (Sharott et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on cited rodent studies.

claim: D2 SPNs were prone to being entrained to parkinsonian β oscillations.
source: In particular, D2 SPNs increased their discharge (Mallet et al., 2006; Sharott et al., 2017) and were also prone to being entrained to parkinsonian β oscillations (Sharott et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on cited rodent studies.

claim: The absolute increase in the discharge rate even of the D2 SPNs was modest (from ~0.5 to ~2.8 Hz).
source: Nevertheless, the absolute increase in the discharge rate even of the D2 SPNs was still modest (from ~0.5 to~2.8 Hz) (Sharott et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on cited rodent studies.

claim: Recent studies have reported no significant increase in the low discharge rate of either SPN subpopulation in striatal dopamine-depleted mice.
source: Moreover, recent studies have reported no significant increase in the low discharge rate of either SPN subpopulation in striatal dopamine-depleted mice (Ketzef et al., 2017; Maltese et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on cited recent rodent studies.

claim: Only one research group has recorded drastic increases in the spontaneous spiking activity in the striatum of PD patients in comparison to either dystonic patients or the normal levels of striatal activity reported in healthy animals.
source: Since only one research group has recorded drastic increases in the spontaneous spiking activity in the striatum of PD patients in comparison to either dystonic patients or the normal levels of striatal activity reported in healthy animals (Singh et al., 2016), we examined our human patient data to determine whether we could report similar changes.
evidence: This is a summary of the literature with citation.

claim: The study utilized a machine learning algorithm to automatically detect striato-pallidal border.
source: Our study goes beyond previous reports (Singh et al., 2016) by utilizing a machine learning algorithm to automatically detect striato-pallidal border, and applying objective methods for the identification of units and the quantification of their isolation quality and stationarity.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the current study.

claim: The study applied objective methods for the identification of units and the quantification of their isolation quality and stationarity.
source: Our study goes beyond previous reports (Singh et al., 2016) by utilizing a machine learning algorithm to automatically detect striato-pallidal border, and applying objective methods for the identification of units and the quantification of their isolation quality and stationarity.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the current study.

claim: Extracellular recording methods cannot discriminate between the spiking activity of striatal D1 and D2 SPNs.
source: Although extracellular recording methods cannot discriminate between the spiking activity of striatal D1 and D2 SPNs, we assumed that if only one population of striatal neurons was strongly affected by the pathological state, we should observe a significantly higher discharge rate of SPNs than that reported in normal NHPs and ET patients, and/or distinct clusters of SPN activity in our patients.
evidence: This is a known limitation of the recording technique.

claim: If only one population of striatal neurons was strongly affected by the pathological state, one should observe a significantly higher discharge rate of SPNs than that reported in normal NHPs and ET patients, and/or distinct clusters of SPN activity.
source: Although extracellular recording methods cannot discriminate between the spiking activity of striatal D1 and D2 SPNs, we assumed that if only one population of striatal neurons was strongly affected by the pathological state, we should observe a significantly higher discharge rate of SPNs than that reported in normal NHPs and ET patients, and/or distinct clusters of SPN activity in our patients.
evidence: This is a logical assumption underlying the analysis approach.

claim: 93 microelectrode trajectories (48 in PD and 45 in Dystonia) were used in the study.
source: In this study, 93 microelectrode trajectories (48 in PD and 45 in Dystonia) were used, yielding a total of 933 and 718 microelectrode recording (MER) segments within the posterior putamen (i.e., posterior to the anterior commissure, Figure 1 and Video 1) of patients suffering from PD and Dystonia, respectively.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: The study yielded a total of 933 and 718 microelectrode recording (MER) segments within the posterior putamen of patients suffering from PD and Dystonia, respectively.
source: In this study, 93 microelectrode trajectories (48 in PD and 45 in Dystonia) were used, yielding a total of 933 and 718 microelectrode recording (MER) segments within the posterior putamen (i.e., posterior to the anterior commissure, Figure 1 and Video 1) of patients suffering from PD and Dystonia, respectively.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study, with reference to figures.

claim: Microelectrode trajectories from patients suffering from non-genetic (N = 27) and genetic (N = 18) Dystonia were pooled, since the results did not differ statistically.
source: Microelectrode trajectories from patients suffering from non-genetic (N = 27) and genetic (N = 18) Dystonia were pooled, since the results did not differ statistically.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision based on statistical analysis.

claim: Applying automatic spike sorting on MER segments identified 5237 units (2917 in PD and 2320 in Dystonia).
source: Applying automatic spike sorting on these MER segments identified 5237 units (2917 in PD and 2320 in Dystonia).
evidence: This describes the results of spike sorting analysis.

claim: The isolation score ranges from 0 (highly noisy) to 1 (perfect isolation).
source: The isolation score (Joshua et al., 2007) - ranging from 0 (i.e., highly noisy) to 1 (i.e., perfect isolation) - was calculated for each of these units.
evidence: This describes a metric used in the analysis with citation.

claim: Injury potentials are often observed during extracellular microelectrode recordings of striatal activity.
source: Moreover, since injury potentials are often observed during extracellular microelectrode recordings of striatal activity (DeLong, 1971), the stationarity of the firing rate and spike amplitude of the well-isolated units (isolation score ≥0.6) was assessed.
evidence: This is a known phenomenon in the field supported by citation.

claim: All surgeries were carried out while the patients were fully awake (no sedation or anesthesia).
source: All surgeries were carried out while the patients were fully awake (no sedation or anesthesia) and the PD patients were off dopaminergic medication (overnight washout >12 hr).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: PD patients were off dopaminergic medication (overnight washout >12 hr) during surgeries.
source: All surgeries were carried out while the patients were fully awake (no sedation or anesthesia) and the PD patients were off dopaminergic medication (overnight washout >12 hr).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: The DBS target was the ventro-posterior-lateral portion of the GPi for all patients.
source: The DBS target was the ventro-posterior-lateral portion of the GPi for all patients, and trajectory angles were only slightly modified according to patient's anatomy.
evidence: This describes the surgical target.

claim: A significant negative correlation between neuronal discharge rate and isolation score was found in the striatum of PD patients (Pearson's r = −0.87 and −0.89 for median and mean discharge rate, respectively, p<0.01).
source: A significant negative correlation between neuronal discharge rate and isolation score was found in the striatum of the PD (Pearson's r = −0.87 and −0.89 for median and mean discharge rate, respectively, p<0.01, Figure 2B) and dystonic (Pearson's r = −0.89 and −0.85 for median and mean discharge rate, respectively, p<0.01, Figure 2B) patients, indicating that the units with the lowest isolation score had the highest discharge rates.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: A significant negative correlation between neuronal discharge rate and isolation score was found in the striatum of dystonic patients (Pearson's r = −0.89 and −0.85 for median and mean discharge rate, respectively, p<0.01).
source: A significant negative correlation between neuronal discharge rate and isolation score was found in the striatum of the PD (Pearson's r = −0.87 and −0.89 for median and mean discharge rate, respectively, p<0.01, Figure 2B) and dystonic (Pearson's r = −0.89 and −0.85 for median and mean discharge rate, respectively, p<0.01, Figure 2B) patients, indicating that the units with the lowest isolation score had the highest discharge rates.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The units with the lowest isolation score had the highest discharge rates.
source: A significant negative correlation between neuronal discharge rate and isolation score was found in the striatum of the PD (Pearson's r = −0.87 and −0.89 for median and mean discharge rate, respectively, p<0.01, Figure 2B) and dystonic (Pearson's r = −0.89 and −0.85 for median and mean discharge rate, respectively, p<0.01, Figure 2B) patients, indicating that the units with the lowest isolation score had the highest discharge rates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis.

claim: The median firing rate of all the sorted striatal units was relatively high (~30–40 Hz) in both diseases.
source: The median firing rate of all the sorted striatal units was relatively high (~30–40 Hz) in both diseases (Figure 3, first column) and consistent (at least for PD) with the values reported by Singh et al., 2016.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The median firing rate of all sorted striatal units is consistent (at least for PD) with the values reported by Singh et al., 2016.
source: The median firing rate of all the sorted striatal units was relatively high (~30–40 Hz) in both diseases (Figure 3, first column) and consistent (at least for PD) with the values reported by Singh et al., 2016.
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published data.

claim: The firing rate of the dystonic patients was significantly lower than the PD firing rate when considering all sorted units (Mann-Whitney U-test, p<0.001).
source: Similarly, the firing rate of the dystonic patients was significantly lower than the PD firing rate (Mann-Whitney U-test, p<0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, first column).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The significant difference in firing rate between PD and dystonic patients disappeared when only comparing the firing rate of the well-isolated units (isolation score ≥0.6).
source: Nevertheless, this significant difference disappeared and the striatal firing rate decreased dramatically when only comparing the firing rate of the well-isolated units (isolation score ≥0.6) (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, first column).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: There was no drastic change in the striatal firing rate of the well-isolated units of the PD and dystonic patients.
source: Hence, there was no drastic change in the striatal firing rate of the well-isolated units of the PD and dystonic patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: The firing rate of the stationary units was significantly lower than the firing rate of the non-stationary units for both PD (Mann-Whitney U-test, p<0.01) and Dystonia (p<0.001).
source: For both PD and Dystonia, the firing rate of the stationary units was significantly lower than the firing rate of the non-stationary units (Mann-Whitney U-test, p<0.01 and 0.001 for PD and dystonic patients, respectively, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: Inclusion of non-stationary units could have erroneously inflated the striatal firing rate in PD and dystonic patients.
source: Thus, inclusion of non-stationary units could have erroneously inflated the striatal firing rate in PD and dystonic patients.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the stationarity analysis.

claim: Removing the non-stationary units reduced the striatal firing rate of the well-isolated units in the striatum of both PD and dystonic patients.
source: Removing the non-stationary units reduced the striatal firing rate of the well-isolated units in the striatum of both PD and dystonic patients (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, first column).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The striatal firing rate remained similar between both diseases after removing non-stationary units.
source: Moreover, the striatal firing rate remained similar between both diseases after this maneuver.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The mean values of the firing rate were systematically higher than the median values, suggesting that the distributions of the firing rate were not normal and were skewed to the right.
source: Equally important, the mean values of the firing rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, first column) were systematically higher than the median values (Figure 3, first column), suggesting that whatever the quality of the isolation and the stationarity of the striatal units, the distributions of the firing rate were not normal and were skewed to the right.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The distributions of the firing rate of the SPNs were not normally distributed, but rather were strongly skewed to the right for both PD and Dystonia.
source: For both PD and Dystonia, and for all levels of spike isolation, the distributions of the firing rate of the SPNs were not normally distributed, but rather were strongly skewed to the right (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The median ± MAD of the discharge rate was 3.85 ± 1.18 Hz for the well-isolated stationary SPNs in PD.

evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The median ± MAD of the discharge rate was 2.55 ± 0.81 Hz for the well-isolated stationary SPNs in Dystonia.
source: The median ± MAD (median absolute deviation) of the discharge rate was 3.85 ± 1.18 Hz and 2.55 ± 0.81 Hz for the well-isolated stationary SPNs in PD and Dystonia respectively - i.e., in the same range as reported for the controls in animal studies and with no significant difference between PD and Dystonia (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The discharge rate of well-isolated stationary SPNs is in the same range as reported for the controls in animal studies.
source: The median ± MAD (median absolute deviation) of the discharge rate was 3.85 ± 1.18 Hz and 2.55 ± 0.81 Hz for the well-isolated stationary SPNs in PD and Dystonia respectively - i.e., in the same range as reported for the controls in animal studies and with no significant difference between PD and Dystonia (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published data.

claim: There was no significant difference in discharge rate between PD and Dystonia for well-isolated stationary SPNs (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05).
source: The median ± MAD (median absolute deviation) of the discharge rate was 3.85 ± 1.18 Hz and 2.55 ± 0.81 Hz for the well-isolated stationary SPNs in PD and Dystonia respectively - i.e., in the same range as reported for the controls in animal studies and with no significant difference between PD and Dystonia (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: There was a significant difference in the coefficient of variation (CV) of the ISIs of all the sorted striatal units between the PD and dystonic patients (Mann-Whitney U-test, p<0.001).
source: Although weak (Figure 3, second column), there was a significant difference in the coefficient of variation (CV) of the ISIs of all the sorted striatal units between the PD and dystonic patients (Mann-Whitney U-test, p<0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, second column).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The difference in CV of ISIs between PD and dystonic patients vanished when only considering the well-isolated or well-isolated stationary units.
source: Nevertheless, as was the case for the striatal firing rate, this difference vanished when only considering the well-isolated or well-isolated stationary units (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, second column).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The distributions of TIHs of the ISIs of the well-isolated stationary units matched the Poisson temporal distribution of the spikes.
source: Moreover, the distributions of TIHs of the ISIs of the well-isolated stationary units matched the Poisson temporal distribution of the spikes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The mean autocorrelograms of the spike trains did not reveal any periodic or bursty firing patterns in the striatal well-isolated stationary units.
source: Accordingly, the mean autocorrelograms of the spike trains did not reveal any periodic or bursty firing patterns in the striatal well-isolated stationary units (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The prevalence of bursts was relatively low in both PD and dystonic patients.
source: Similarly, the prevalence of bursts [detected using the Poisson surprise method with the surprise maximization (SM) search algorithm (Legéndy and Salcman, 1985), see Materials and methods] was relatively low (Figure 6C) and did not differ significantly between PD and dystonic patients (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The prevalence of bursts did not differ significantly between PD and dystonic patients (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05).
source: Similarly, the prevalence of bursts [detected using the Poisson surprise method with the surprise maximization (SM) search algorithm (Legéndy and Salcman, 1985), see Materials and methods] was relatively low (Figure 6C) and did not differ significantly between PD and dystonic patients (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: Comparison of the power spectral densities (PSDs) of the spiking activities recorded in the striatum of the PD and dystonic patients did not reveal any oscillatory phenomena between 3 and 75 Hz, including the β (13–30 Hz) band.
source: Comparison of the power spectral densities (PSDs) of the spiking activities recorded in the striatum of the PD and dystonic patients did not reveal any oscillatory phenomena between 3 and 75 Hz, including the β (13–30 Hz) band (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the spectral analysis.

claim: No significant difference in the β power of the striatal spiking activities was observed between PD and dystonic patients (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05).
source: Accordingly, no significant difference in the β power of the striatal spiking activities (whatever the quality of the isolation and the stationary of the striatal units) was observed between PD and dystonic patients (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05, Figure 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, third column)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: No significant increases of the β (13–30 Hz) power in the spiking activities recorded in the vicinity of the striatal well-isolated stationary units compared to the linearly interpolated baseline β power were found (Wilcoxon signed rank test, p>0.05).
source: Moreover, we found no significant increases of the β (13–30 Hz) power in the spiking activities recorded in the vicinity of the striatal well-isolated stationary units compared to the linearly interpolated baseline β power (Wilcoxon signed rank test, p>0.05, Figure 7C), thus supporting the claim of no oscillatory spiking activity in the striatum of PD and dystonic patients.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The mean PSD of the mono-polar LFPs recorded in the striatum of PD patients exhibited two distinct peaks (at 11 and 21 Hz).
source: The mean PSD of the mono-polar LFPs recorded in the striatum of PD and dystonic patients (Figure 8A) exhibited (ignoring 50 Hz artifacts) two and three distinct peaks, respectively (at 11 and 21 Hz for PD patients and 8, 22 and 30 Hz for dystonic patients, Figure 8A, insets).
evidence: This is a finding from the spectral analysis of LFPs.

claim: The mean PSD of the mono-polar LFPs recorded in the striatum of dystonic patients exhibited three distinct peaks (at 8, 22 and 30 Hz).
source: The mean PSD of the mono-polar LFPs recorded in the striatum of PD and dystonic patients (Figure 8A) exhibited (ignoring 50 Hz artifacts) two and three distinct peaks, respectively (at 11 and 21 Hz for PD patients and 8, 22 and 30 Hz for dystonic patients, Figure 8A, insets).
evidence: This is a finding from the spectral analysis of LFPs.

claim: The β power in the LFPs recorded around the time of the spikes of all the striatal sorted units was significantly higher in PD than in dystonic patients (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.001).
source: The β power in the LFPs recorded around the time of the spikes of all the striatal sorted units was significantly higher in PD than in dystonic patients (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.001, Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, fourth column).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The difference in β power in LFPs between PD and dystonic patients disappeared when using the spikes of the well-isolated (non-stationary and stationary or only stationary) units.
source: However, this difference disappeared when using the spikes of the well-isolated (non-stationary and stationary or only stationary) units (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, fourth column).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The spiking activity of well-isolated stationary units recorded in the striatum of both PD and dystonic patients failed to lock with 13–30 Hz LFP oscillations.
source: Thus, the spiking activity of well-isolated stationary units recorded in the striatum of both PD and dystonic patients failed to lock with 13–30 Hz LFP oscillations (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a finding from the spike-LFP analysis.

claim: The 3D-classifications of the putative SPNs and TANs, using their firing rate, the CV of their ISI and the score of the first principal component (PC1) of their spike waveform did not clearly discriminate them in either PD or dystonic patients.
source: The 3D-classifications of the putative SPNs and TANs, using their firing rate, the CV of their ISI and the score of the first principal component (PC1) of their spike waveform did not clearly discriminate them in either PD or dystonic patients (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the classification analysis.

claim: The averaged spike waveform hardly varied between putative SPNs and TANs in either PD or dystonic patients.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that the averaged spike waveform hardly varied between these two subtypes of striatal units in either PD or dystonic patients (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the waveform analysis.

claim: No significant differences were found in the firing rate of the putative SPNs and TANs in PD patients.
source: Besides, we did not find significant differences in the firing rate of the putative SPNs and TANs in PD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D, first column) or dystonic (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D, first column) patients.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: No significant differences were found in the firing rate of the putative SPNs and TANs in dystonic patients.
source: Besides, we did not find significant differences in the firing rate of the putative SPNs and TANs in PD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D, first column) or dystonic (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D, first column) patients.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The CV of the ISI was significantly smaller for the putative TANs than for the putative SPNs in both diseases.
source: However, the CV of the ISI was significantly smaller for the putative TANs than for the putative SPNs in both diseases (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D, second column), thus corroborating the view that TANs fire in a more regular fashion than the SPNs which are thought to be phasically activated (Crutcher and DeLong, 1984; Deffains et al., 2010; Kimura et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The proportions of outliers (regardless of the spiking feature and the isolation level) were small.
source: Nevertheless, we found that the proportions of outliers (regardless of the spiking feature and the isolation level) were small (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the outlier analysis.

claim: No significant disease effect on the proportions (chi-square test, p>0.05) or the values (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05) of outliers was found when only considering the well-isolated or well-isolated stationary units.
source: Moreover, we did not find any significant disease effect on the proportions (chi-square test, p>0.05) or the values (Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05) of these outliers when only considering the well-isolated or well-isolated stationary units (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the outlier analysis.

claim: The two predefined clusters from k-means analysis were not well-separated, regardless of the quality of the isolation or the stationarity of the striatal units.
source: The results showed that the two predefined clusters were not well-separated, regardless of the quality of the isolation or the stationarity of the striatal units (Figure 9, insets).
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis.

claim: The tendency to burst (CV of the ISIs > 1) decreased for units with a high discharge rate.
source: Equally important, in contrast with the view that discharge rate elevation and bursting activity coexist in the striatum of PD patients (Singh et al., 2016), the tendency to burst (CV of the ISIs > 1; Kaneoke and Vitek, 1996) decreased for units with a high discharge rate (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis that contradicts a previous view.

claim: The results in patients extend the authors' previous study in the MPTP NHP model of PD.
source: In conclusion, our results in patients extend our previous study in the MPTP NHP model of PD (Deffains et al., 2016) and studies in the 6-OHDA rodent model (e.g., Ketzef et al., 2017; Maltese et al., 2019) and demonstrate that abnormal activity along both the direct and indirect pathways of the BG network is not caused by drastic changes in spontaneous SPN spiking activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement connecting current findings to previous work.

claim: Abnormal activity along both the direct and indirect pathways of the BG network is not caused by drastic changes in spontaneous SPN spiking activity.
source: In conclusion, our results in patients extend our previous study in the MPTP NHP model of PD (Deffains et al., 2016) and studies in the 6-OHDA rodent model (e.g., Ketzef et al., 2017; Maltese et al., 2019) and demonstrate that abnormal activity along both the direct and indirect pathways of the BG network is not caused by drastic changes in spontaneous SPN spiking activity.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Maltese et al., 2019 reported abnormal recruitment of D1 and D2 SPNs during behavior in parkinsonism that resulted in an aberrant net balance of striatal outputs, although there were no changes in the firing rate of the individual neurons.
source: Recently, Maltese et al., 2019 reported abnormal recruitment (e.g., during behavior) of D1 and D2 SPNs (which are mostly silent at rest in the healthy condition) in parkinsonism that resulted in an aberrant net balance of striatal outputs, although there were no changes in the firing rate of the individual neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: It is likely that small to moderate changes in spontaneous SPN discharge are amplified by BG downstream structures, thus leading to the clinical symptoms of PD and possibly of Dystonia.
source: It is likely that these small to moderate changes in spontaneous SPN discharge are amplified by BG downstream structures (Crompe et al., 2020), thus leading to the clinical symptoms of PD and possibly of Dystonia.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.
